content: Chiggers, also known as chigoes, refer to two types of parasitic arthropods with similar behaviors. The first is the chigoe flea (Tunga penetrans), which is commonly found in tropical climates. The second is the larva of a harvest mite, which can carry a microscopic parasite called Orientia tsutsugamushi that causes scrub typhus. These larvae are also referred to as scrub mites, red mites, and by other names. They are distributed across temperate and tropical regions. The term chigger originated as a variation of chigoe, but in North America, it most commonly refers to the harvest mite. Pathophysiology Chiggers do not burrow into the skin, nor do they feed on blood. Instead, they attach to their host and inject digestive enzymes into the bite site. These enzymes break down the host's tissue, which the chigger then consumes. Warm, rainy conditions promote the reproduction of these parasitic and predatory mites, leading to large populations. When ground temperatures consistently exceed 60°F, harvest mites lay eggs, marking the beginning of chigger season. Chiggers avoid sunlight and high humidity. During wet seasons, they are typically found in tall grass and vegetation, while in dry seasons, they are more commonly located under brush and in shaded areas. Treatment To alleviate itching caused by chigger bites, apply an anti-itch cream containing hydrocortisone, calamine, or benzyl benzoate. If you are sensitive to these medications or have concerns, consult your healthcare provider or pharmacist for guidance. Prevention Maintain short grass in your yard. Remove brush and wood debris where potential mite hosts may reside. Keep major hosts, such as rodents and small mammals, away from the area. Secure trash cans to discourage wildlife from approaching your home. Allow sunlight to penetrate the grass, as this will dry the lawn and make it less hospitable for chiggers. Apply insect repellent to your feet, legs, and midsection to reduce the risk of chigger bites.
